en: The Commentary on the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi* entitled *Mahāsukhaprakāśikā*, edited by Banarasī Lāla. Om! Homage to the venerable Bhagavatī Vajravārāhī! May the Blessed Lady Vajravilāsinī protect the three worlds from misfortune—she who has emerged as the Fortune of the Perfectly Awakened One from the ornament of the ocean of bliss; she who is endowed with all forms of excellence and destroys the mass of darkness that is the world’s evil; she who is the steadfastness of the treasury of the knowledge of light, the tranquility of the treasury of mindfulness, and the wisdom of the treasury of intellect.
Having paid homage to the row of pollen-dust from the lotus-feet of the illustrious Vajradevī, and to the feet of my Guru,
I [expound] the illustrious Saṃvara, the concealed bodhicitta, the praised state of the non-duality of wisdom and compassion.
By the monk Dhyānacandra, who abides in the bliss of prostrating at the pair of feet of Vajradevī, and by Candrivasu-vaśarman.
The means for achieving the goal of Vajravārāhī is here briefly analyzed for one's own benefit;
may my mind always be eager for the conceptualization of well-spoken words.
Therefore, this has been composed by me, whose intellect is dull and very limited, with great faith;
the great people should not look for faults in me.

The master Śrī Śūnyatāsamādhivajrapāda, desiring to compose the *sādhana* of Śrī Vajradevī, first composed two verses of benediction by way of manifesting the nature and qualities of the Blessed Lady,
beginning with "Udyātā" and so forth.

May Vārāhikā protect you— she who has emerged from the circle of the navel, who is radiant with flashes of lightning stirred by the wind, who has consumed the three types of enemies, who is honored by the three worlds, who is drenched in streams of nectar, who is permeated by the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom, who is stainless, who bestows a mass of her own bliss, and who is free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence. || 1 ||
The grammatical connection is: "May Vārāhī protect you. She is called Vārāhī because she brings forth (*āhinoti*) the excellent (*vara*) thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*);
[this is derived from] the root *hi*, meaning "to go," with the prefix *ā*.
The suffix *aṇ* (or *kan*) is applied by virtue of the term *saṃjñā*; the substitution of *ā* for *a* occurs because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
The meaning is that he follows after the Blessed One who resides in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Because there is no difference between the Bodhicitta and the Bhagavatī.
Of what nature is the Bhagavatī?
She is "risen," having gone upward.
Why? From the navel-center (tala-cakra) and the emanation-center (nirmāṇa-cakra).
"Shaken by the wind" means agitated by that wind known as the downward-moving breath (apāna).
"Radiant like flashes of lightning."
She is like lightning—passionate yet stainless.
By her, the three enemies have been burnt; by the word "enemy" (ari), the wheel is designated.
That which is called the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Mahāsukha wheels has been burnt through the departure of their conceptual constructions.
"Worshipped by the three worlds" means she who is honored and venerated by the three worlds—the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Alternatively, she is worshipped by the Tathāgatas residing in the [mandala] circles, who are themselves "worlds"; for this very reason, she is "bathed in a stream of nectar," where "nectar" refers to the *bodhicitta*, and she is "bathed" or sprinkled by its stream.
Externally, worship is also performed with water and other offerings;
here, the maintenance of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) itself constitutes the ritual bath with water.

"Intoxicated by the flavor of the Buddha-gnosis": the Buddha-gnosis is free from conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence; that itself is the "flavor," and she is "intoxicated" by it, meaning pervaded by it, because the Blessed Lady consists of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).
For this very reason it is "unstained," since the stain is said to be the emission of the *bodhicitta*.
For this very reason, detachment arises.

According to the scriptural teaching: "From falling away, detachment is produced; from detachment, suffering arises. That which brings about cyclic existence through karma is itself suffering, and that karma arises precisely from falling away.
And thus it is said: "There is no merit higher than dispassion, and nothing superior to happiness.
It bestows a mass of bliss; that is, a mass of bliss (*ānanda-sandoha*) that is truly its own (*sva*). The phrase "to all people" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

It is devoid of the investigation into existence and non-existence; "existence" is the grasping at permanence, and "non-existence" is the grasping at annihilation—the investigation of these two is what is meant here—and it is free from such investigation because it is filled with absolute bliss. || 1 ||

May Vārāhikā— who resides within the solar mandala of the emanation wheel, who is encircled by the letters beginning with *ka*, who is ablaze with the brilliance of a flaming fire yet drinks the nectar of immortality, who is like a fine lotus fiber, who as the *vidyā* burns away the assembly of Buddhas by piercing the three wheels, and who moves gracefully upward in bliss— shine forth in my mind.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nirmāṇālī" and so forth:
the syntactical connection is that Vārāhikā may manifest within your hearts.
"Situated upon the solar mandala of the emanation line" means she is situated upon the solar mandalas of the emanation wheel, the enjoyment wheel, and the wheel of great bliss.
This Vajravārāhī, whose nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), is enveloped by the letters beginning with *ka* and so forth; she is the Blessed Lady who pervades all that is external.
She is blazing with a radiant fire because her form is exceedingly luminous and because she burns away all the darkness of sin.

"Amṛtasavā" means she whose bath (*sava*) is with the nectar (*amṛta*), which is the *bodhicitta*. "Like a fine lotus-fiber" means she who has the likeness of a fine lotus-fiber, that is, a lotus-stalk fiber (*mṛṇāla-sūtra*).
This is because she has the nature of the *avadhūtī* and because she indicates the knowledge of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-jñāna*).

The *vidyā* burns the assembly of Buddhas; that *vidyā* refers to Locanā and the others, whose intrinsic nature is earth and the other elements, while the Buddhas refer to Vairocana and the others. It burns their union and causes one to enter into non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Thus it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The *caṇḍālī*, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas."
When Locanā and the others are burned, the moon flows forth once it has been consumed.
And thus, this Blessed Lady is Caṇḍālī in her essential nature;
she pierces the three wheels by ascending through the Dharmacakra, Sambhogacakra, and Mahāsukhacakra.
For this very reason, she is Anandā (Blissful) and Lalitā (Graceful), due to the arising of the excellence of all forms.
They are "upward-moving" because they constantly proceed upward toward the wheel of great bliss. || 2 ||
Having prostrated with my head before Vajravārāhī, the Vajrayoginī who is preceded by the Vajra,
I shall speak for the sake of my own recollection the accomplishment of the knowledge of reality.
"Having prostrated," and so forth.
The connection is: "I shall explain the complete attainment of the knowledge of reality.
Its intrinsic nature is reality (*tattva*).

Because it is said that "the characteristic of non-arising is the reality of non-arising," I shall describe the perfect accomplishment of the knowledge— that is, the correct realization— of that [reality], having prostrated to Vajravārāhī, who is preceded by "Vajra" (meaning Vārāhī).
She is Vajrayoginī because she possesses yoga with "Vajra," which is the wisdom of non-apprehension.
"With my head" means with the crown of the head.
"For what purpose shall I speak? means for the sake of my own memory, that is, for the sake of recollecting myself.
This is precisely the avoidance of arrogance on the part of the excellent teacher. (3)

[The Procedure for External Worship] Having entered a secluded place favorable to the mind, seated upon a soft cushion there, the wise one, supported by the lap of the Lord, should contemplate purification. (4)
First, he speaks of the perfection of the place.
The connection is that one should cultivate purity, beginning with the words "solitary" and so forth;
the meaning is that one should meditate upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

According to the principle that "the purity of all things is considered to be suchness (*tathatā*)," the sole purpose of meditating on emptiness is the abandonment of the entire mass of conceptual constructions accumulated since beginningless time.
Having entered a secluded place devoid of people, one should remain alone for the sake of concentrating the mind; as for this secluded place, it may be of any kind whatsoever.
Not for the sake of concentrating the mind. Therefore he says: having done what, does the stability of the mind occur in that which is favorable to the mind?

Having sat upon a seat—since even an ordinary seat does not bring happiness, it is therefore specified as "sukumāram," meaning soft—what further qualifies it? It is "sannāthāṅkakaḥ": marked (aṅkita) or characterized by the Lord (nātha), who is one's own Guru; that which is marked by him is soft.
What further qualifies it? It is "sannāthāṅkakaḥ": he whose head (śiraḥ) is marked or characterized by the Lord, his own Guru, is "nāthāṅkakaḥ."
Alternatively, [it means] one whose head is marked by Vairocana;
"sudhīḥ" means a wise scholar,
because only one who is intelligent has the qualification for such a matter.
Now, the distinction is explained: "solitary" (*vijana*) means that where there is no perception of people, it is solitary; the meaning is that its characteristic is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
For this very reason, it is "conducive to the mind," because the world abides in great bliss alone.
Because of the statement, "The world consists of all that is blissful," the wise one should enter while embracing the Lord. Having sat there upon a soft seat, he should contemplate purity.

"Nāthāṅkaka" means one who has the mark of the Lord (nātha) as his crest; the Lord is the Vajra-Guru, and his "mark" (aṅka) is the sign of the fourth moment (*kṣaṇa*). He in whom there is bliss (*ka*) therein is "Nāthāṅka," and for that reason, he is "Sudhī" (the wise one). Yet, even that is dependent upon a cause. Regarding that, he states the cause: "having sat upon a delicate seat. "Seat" (*āsana*) refers to the *dharmodayā*.
By the word "delicate" (*sukumāra*), he indicates one endowed with the prime of youth, because it is precisely therein that the arising of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) occurs.
Having sat down and entered into union,
it is said here: if even that pleasure is dependent upon causes, then how can that pleasure be called "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*)?
Whatever is dependent upon causes is impermanent;
how, then, can that be happiness?
And thus it is said: "For the impermanent, suffering is certain; that which is accompanied by suffering is not happiness."

To this it is replied: This is true; however, it is "with a cause. That which was stated refers to the conventional understanding of the relationship between cause and effect as perceived by the world.
Thus, the venerable Ācārya Devapāda said: "Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand by means of any other language..."
In that same way, the world cannot be made to grasp [the truth] without recourse to worldly conventions.
Thus,
that bliss which is characterized by non-arising is conceptualized as being either accompanied by time or devoid of time,
because it is not within the range of the intellect.

"Reality is beyond the scope of the intellect"—according to this principle, it is established that the designation of the relationship between cause and effect exists only within the conventional realm. || 4 ||
Thereafter, having inscribed the heart-mantra of Vajradhara with the six-syllable mantra recited three times, one should honor it with red flowers using the ring finger.
Thereafter, and so forth:
one should worship the heart of Vajradhara with red flowers.
"Vajra" refers to indivisible gnosis; he who holds that is Vajradhara.
He is the Samyaksambuddha. Because his heart is not to be revealed, it is called Dharmodayā.
It should be worshipped with red flowers such as the *karavīra* and others.
"Having scraped with the ring finger" means with the ring finger of the left hand.
"By the sixth Jina": the sixth Jina, Vajrasattva, is designated as the "substance" (*dravya*), because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause, since it arises from him.
"Recited with the three syllables" means recited with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.
This is the second meaning.

Having drawn the lotus-heart of the Perfectly Awakened Vajradhara with the ring finger, one should move it with the [thumb acting as a] vajra; and thus says the venerable Lord Saṃvara: "The knower of yoga should always lick [the substance] with the faces of the ring finger and the thumb."
The sixth Vajrasattva is [designated] by the sixth Jina because he is the cause of its arising.
Bodhicitta itself is designated as Vajrasattva through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause.
By means of that [Bodhicitta], which serves as the defining characteristic...

But the *bodhicitta* located within the interior of the lotus of wisdom must not be emitted, because at that time great bliss (*mahāsukha*) would not arise. Thus it is said in the *Ādibuddha*: "When the *bodhicitta*, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen..."
When the aggregates and consciousness have fainted, how can there be any blameless accomplishment?
Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that one should worship with a red flower—that is, one should perform the adoration with its pollen—by means of that which has been consecrated by the recitation (*japta*) of the three syllables, which is of a single nature through the non-duality of body, speech, and mind, and which has entered the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). || 5 ||
Thereafter, having placed the right hand (the lotus-hand) into the vessel of Paramādya,
one should perform the vajra-sipping according to the oral instruction by touching it with the tongue.
Following that, "in the vessel of Paramādya," and so forth;
the connection is that one should perform the *vajra-savana* (the vajra-bath).
*Vajra* is non-apprehending gnosis (*anupalambha-jñāna*); because it is the cause for its arising, the physical substance itself is designated by that term.
Therefore, one should perform the ritual bathing and washing.

Regarding the phrase "in the supreme primordial vessel" and so forth: the *vajrasavana* (diamond-bath) is performed by casting [the water] from the hand-lotus; that is to say, having cast it from the hand-lotus, one uses the "other than the right," meaning the left hand.

In the vessel of Paramādya, there is the substance of Paramādya; its vessel is that [vessel], and therein, according to the instruction—that is, without transgressing the instruction—one purifies the substance with the three syllables. By the touch of the hand, this is the intended meaning:
because of the satiation of the host of deities held in the hands.
Therein, on the ring finger is HĀṂ YOṂ;
on the index finger is HRĪṂ MOṂ;
on the middle finger is HREṂ HRĪṂ.
Having placed *huṃ hraṃ* on the ring finger,
*phaṭ phaṭ* on the little finger,
and *oṃ vaṃ* in the center of the hand, and having offered libations, one should visualize the substance as one's own limbs and members by means of the mantra of the Bhagavatī with the left hand.

The second meaning: "In the supreme primary vessel" (*paramādyapātre*). It is "supreme" (*parama*) because of its excellence; it is "primary" (*ādya*) because it is the initial cause of bliss; and it is specifically called a "vessel" (*pātra*) because it serves as the support for that bliss.
This is designated as the lotus of knowledge (*vidyā-paṅkaja*).

In that regard, with the vessel serving as the causal sign (*nimitta*), the "hand-lotus" (*karakamala*) is so called because it bestows (*rāti*) ease (*ka*); thus, the *bodhicitta* arises. That very lotus is [called] "excellent" (*kara*) because it is fully blossomed, desirable, and endowed with supreme qualities.
For this very reason, it is the "other than the right" (*dakṣiṇetara*); for even in the right [nostril], there is the element of passion (*rajo-dhātu*).

Then, having cast the "moon-element" (*candra-dhātu*)—the syllable *haṃ*—into the other, one should direct the mind like the *avadhūti* upward and perform the "vajra-sound. When the *bodhicitta* has reached the *avadhūti*, it is then designated as the "vajra."
By that, one should perform the hearing and the bathing;
one should lead the *bodhicitta* to the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).

"According to the instruction" means according to the guru’s instruction; here, the feet of the guru are to be taken as refuge. Through the touch of the body—that is, by touching the breasts of the consort with the hand—that very mind becomes possessed of passion (*sarāga*).
And when the mind becomes possessed of passion, at that very moment there is the expansion of the avadhūtī;
and when there is the expansion of the avadhūtī, then the bodhicitta pervades the wheel of great bliss. || 6 ||
Having performed the *karanyāsa* by joining the thumb with the fingers,
one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* using the six mantras of Vīreśvarī.
"Having performed," and so forth; the connection is "one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*.
Having performed the *karanyāsa*—that is, having performed the *karanyāsa* with the mantras of the six deities according to the stated sequence—...
By joining the thumb and finger of the right hand, one should take the substance with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand, smear it on the hands,
and then perform the *aṅganyāsa* (limb-assignment) with the six *Vīreśvarī* mantras.
Therein, *oṃ vaṃ* at the navel is the indicator of the goddess Vārāhī, who is red in color.

Hāṃ yāṃ at the heart, marked by the blue-colored goddess Yāminī; Hrīṃ moṃ at the face, marked by the white-colored goddess Mohinī; Hreṃ hrīṃ at the head, marked by the yellow-colored goddess Saṃcāriṇī.

One should place the mantra-syllable *huṃ hūṃ* on the topknot (*śikhā*), which characterizes the goddess *Saṃtrāsinī* who is green in color; and the mantra-syllable *phaṭ phaṭ* on the forehead (*lalāṭa*), which characterizes the goddess *Caṇḍikā* who is smoke-colored.
This is because there is no distinction between the mantra and its deity.
Alternatively, those very syllables should be meditated upon as deities through the transformation of each respective syllable.

Thus, Vajravārāhī is red in color, with three faces and six arms; her root face is red, the left blue, and the right green. She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in her left [hands], and a noose in her [other] left; she holds a hook, a Brahma-head, and a flaying knife in her right hands. She stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. Yāminī is blue in color, with one face and four arms; she holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a bell in her left [hands].
On the right, they hold a *ḍamaru* drum and a flaying knife.

Mohanī, Saṃcāriṇī, Saṃtrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā are white, yellow, green, and smoke-colored respectively; each has one face and four arms. In the left hands of all of them are a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a bell; in the right hands are a *ḍamaru* and a flaying knife. All have wide-striding steps (*ālīḍhapada*), loose hair, and three eyes. She who is white possesses the luster of the moon and is marked by a lunar disc; the others possess the luster of the sun and are marked by solar discs.
The second meaning: *Kara* is that which produces (*karoti*) bliss (*kaṃ*), namely the *bodhicitta*; its *nyāsa* is its pervading of all limbs through the union of the thumb and fingers.

Because of the statement, "The knower of yoga should always lick [it] with the mouth of the ring finger and the thumb through the union of the lotus of wisdom and the excellent vajra," one should do so.
Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the *bodhicitta*;
rather, one should indeed meditate upon the image of the Buddha throughout the entire threefold world without exception.
According to this principle:
one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the six mantras of Vīreśvarī.
This consists of the form of the Pure Bhagavatī, which is composed of the atoms of the six deities to be described hereafter.

Immediately after emptiness—that is, following the meditation on emptiness—one should visualize the form of the glorious Vajradevī; having performed the placement of the limbs of protection (*ārakṣāṅga-nyāsa*) and so forth, one should write the heart-mantra of Vajradhara and worship it with red flowers—this is how it should be understood. (7)
Thereafter, one should slowly sprinkle upon the Vajradhara [the image] a mantra of equal measure produced from vermilion and mercury,
using excellent powders derived from serpents contained within a cloth.
And following that, "above Vajradhara," and so forth;
the connection is with the phrase "one should scatter the mantraless.
The "mantraless" refers to the vessel.

*Raṅgārūṇayogajaṃ* means produced from the combination of *raṅga* (tin) and *arūṇa* (copper); *yoga* refers to their union or melting together, and that which is born therefrom is *kāṃsya* (bell-metal). It is called "equal" (*sama*) because it is free from defects such as unevenness. Where should one scatter [the powder]? "Upon the bearer of the thunderbolt" (*vajradharopari*); a "thunderbolt-bearer" (*vajradhara*) is one who holds the substance *vajra*; thus, it means upon the human skull joined with the *madana* plant.
"Born of serpents" (*bhujagabhavaiḥ*); a "serpent" (*bhujaga*) is a *nāga*, meaning tin (*śīśaka*).
In this context, "with excellent, superior vermilion" refers to that which is contained within the garments (*sicaya*), meaning situated inside the clothes.

Here is the instruction: one should gently sprinkle a bell-metal vessel with superior vermilion from a garment stained with menstrual blood, using a swinging mechanism (*dolāpaṭayantra*) and the index finger; this is done for the sake of stability.
This is the second meaning.

He is called Vajradhara because he holds the *vajra*, which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). The "lotus of wisdom" (*prajñāpaṅkaja*) refers to that [lotus]; "born from the union of *raṅga* and *aruṇa*" means produced therefrom. *Raṅga* is endowed with passion (*rāga*), while *maṇyagram* (the tip of the jewel) is indeed like the dawn, hence *aruṇa*. The "filament of the lotus of knowledge" (*vidyāpadyakiñjalka*) refers to those two; their "union" (*yoga*) is their meeting. "Born from the union of *raṅga* and *aruṇa*" means the bodhicitta accompanied by great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Therefore, it is "without mantra" because it is equal [to all], and "beyond mantra" because it is the foundation of all knowledge; the meaning is that one should scatter it with vermilion pigments produced from serpents.
The meaning is that they are "well-fastened," as if upon a garment, by means of most excellent great dyes; "gradually" means step by step. || 8 ||
Having accurately drawn the *jina-hṛdaya-cakra* with a tip like a peacock feather,
one should inscribe the row of mantras within its center using a probe made of gold from the Ganges.
Regarding the passage beginning with "there," the connection is that one should draw the *mantrālī*.
Having drawn the *cakra*, the term *śikhikoṭika* means that which has a "peak" (*koṭi*) like that of a "crested one" (*śikhin*), namely fire; thus, it refers to a triangle.

Herein is the instruction: one should draw the six-spoked wheel, which is the heart of the Jina—the heart of the Fully Awakened One (Sambuddha), the heart of that [deity], because it is the cause for the arising of secret gnosis (*guhyajñāna*).
Within its womb, in the center of that wheel, this mantra should be written with a rod of gold or a rod of *gāṅgeya* (yellow orpiment) using the left hand alone.
This is the second meaning.

The *jinahṛdaya* (the heart of the Victors) is the heart, which is the lotus of knowledge (*vidyākamala*) and indeed that very wheel (*cakra*), because it is the abode of the wisdom of all the Victors.
It is "peaked with a crest" (*śikhikoṭika*) because its peak is the crest of the Victor, being the nature of the brilliance at the tip of wisdom.

Having drawn this well with a vajra and having brought it into union, [one draws] that which has a womb within it—that is, the wheel of excellent emanation (*sunirmāṇacakra*) within its interior; this is the meaning of "on the base" (*tala*).

One should write the *mantrālī*; "mantra" is so called because it protects the mind (*manaḥ-saṃtrāṇāt*), and its *ālī* is the row or sequence of *bodhicitta*. One should apply that stream of *bodhicitta* with a golden probe (*gāṅgeya-śalākayā*).
Because the *avadhūtī* is golden-red and because the *avadhūtī* is also possessed of passion (*sarāga*), it is therefore similar to a golden probe. 9.
On the outer part of the wheel, in the directions of the east, north, west, and south,
one should draw six svastikas in sequence with the left hand.
"Of the wheel," and so forth;
the connection is that one should draw auspicious svastikas.
"The nandyāvarta" refers to the outer portion of the wheel.

In the directions of the east, north, west, and south (arkidig), one should draw svastikas with the left hand, either in the sequence of east, north, west, and south, or by circling counter-clockwise.
The second meaning is that on the outer part of the wheel, outside the *nirmāṇacakra*, in all the directions of the east, north, west, and south—one should draw them everywhere.
One should draw the svastikas.
A beautiful svastika is the posture in which one should maintain concentration everywhere.
Gradually, very slowly;
with the left hand, the hand is held in the practice of dhāraṇā; by virtue of its similarity to that, the hand is [like] the wind (ma).
"By the thief" means by that which is situated in the left nostril-passage. || 10 ||
"Having drawn in," and so forth;
the connection is that one should satisfy the Vajradevī.

Having drawn in—that is, having summoned and caused to enter—the Blessed Lady who dwells in the Akaniṣṭha realm, one binds her by means of the syllables of the mantra according to the ritual procedure.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having formed the *jvālāmudrā*, one should rotate it over the forehead in a counter-clockwise direction while gazing upward. Reciting the syllable *phaṭ* first, and then reciting *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, [one performs the following]:

by *jaḥ* there is summoning; by *hūṃ*, entry; by *vaṃ*, binding; and by *hoḥ*, pleasing. The second meaning is: having summoned the Vajra Goddess in the form of Caṇḍālī, and having drawn her into the *avadhūtī*, one binds her within the mantra-syllables. Then, having made the mantra—the *bodhicitta*—and its syllables—which are emptiness—one's own nature, [one unites with her].
One should satisfy [the deity] according to the prescribed ritual.
One should perform this again and again in this manner.
The rest is easy to understand according to the specific details. 11.

Thereafter, one should perform various forms of worship for her who exists in the form of mantra, with foods to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and sucked, endowed with all desirable qualities. 12.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadanu" and so forth: the connection is that one should "perform worship" (saparyā vidadhīta).
The meaning is that one should perform the ritual of adoration (pūjām vidadhyāt).

The various great [offerings] for that Vajradevī, who is in the form of mantra, are preceded by the application of vermilion (sindūra) upon the surface of a mirror; the remainder is easy to understand. "With the qualities of desire" means with those that are most excellent.
This is the second meaning.
The sense is that one should perform *saparyā*, which means worship; this should be understood as *bodhicitta*.
It is "various," being fashioned from an uninterrupted stream of *bodhicitta*, and takes the form of mantra, having emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its intrinsic nature.

"With foods," and so forth, means with [objects of] form and the rest; "with the qualities of desire" means accompanied by great bliss (*mahāsukha*). This very worship is for the sake of pacifying all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). || 12 ||
With various forces accompanied by intoxication, with five most excellent offerings, and with songs, instrumental music, dances, circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise; || 13 ||
"By various," and so forth:

by various forces—that is, by many forces—by offerings consisting of meats together with *madana* and other substances, by the five [grains], namely mung beans, black gram, lentils, peas, and wheat; or else, by form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, which are most excellent and supreme.
With songs, vajra-songs, musical instruments such as the lute, and dances, vajra-step dances, as well as circumambulations, prostrations, and praises—this is easy to understand.
This is the second meaning.

One must effect the entry into non-apprehension together with the "forces," namely the five aggregates and the heaps of flesh; therefore, with the "intoxicants," which are the bodhicitta arrived at the presence of great bliss, the remainder is according to the literal text. 13.
One who desires her accomplishment should perform the prescribed ritual of worship on the tenth lunar day, whether daily, every fortnight, or monthly. (14)
"Every day," and so forth.
The connection is that one should perform the ritual of worship as described.
Whether daily, or every fortnight, or every month, or on the tenth lunar day (*tithi*), or...

The wise one, desiring the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of this Vajrayoginī and keeping in mind both mundane and supramundane accomplishments, [should understand] that the intention is this: "This very Blessed Lady bestows the entire mass of all happiness. (14)

Thus ends the first chapter, the Ritual for External Worship, in the *Mahāsukhaprakāśikā* commentary composed by the monk Śrī Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Middle Way, for the sake of perfecting the knowledge of reality. || 1 ||

[The Procedure for Meditation] Now, having performed the external rite of worship, one who possesses great compassion should meditate upon the previously described Goddess, whose form is like that of the sun’s orb, seated in the center of a lotus within the heart of the enemy he has created. 1.
Now, the procedure for the meditation on Vajravārāhī is described.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" (now) and so forth, the connection is: "one should meditate upon the Goddess."
One should meditate upon that which was previously described and spoken by the Tathāgatas, beginning with Dīpaṃkara and Śākyamuni, or otherwise, as it was described at the time of prior cultivation.
"Possessing great compassion" means having vast compassion; "bodhicitta" means one whose body is fully perfected.
[He is] the emanated enemy.
"In the lotus of the center" means in the lotus at the center of the *nirmāṇacakra*.

"The orb of the sun whose life-breaths have departed" means: he whose *asavaḥ* (life-breaths) have departed is *vyasuḥ*; his *hṛdayam* (heart). He whose rays (*gau*) are hot (*uṣṇaḥ*) is *uṣṇaguḥ*; his *bimbam* (orb) is the *uṣṇagubimbam*. This is the meaning of "the orb of the sun whose heart-life has departed. This refers to her own heart and the orb of the sun.

One should meditate on the Blessed Lady upon a sun-disc at the heart of a corpse above the *nirmāṇacakra*. This is what is meant: when the *bodhicitta*, having reached the tip of the jewel, returns and reaches the *nirmāṇacakra*, a certain kind of bliss arises; that which indicates this is the "corpse" (*śava*), its "heart" (*hṛdaya*) being emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The sun-disc, however, symbolizes the sun of non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*), because it destroys the darkness of all conceptual constructions.
Therein, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lady, Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. || 1 ||

Of what nature is she? She has the color of vermilion at twilight; she possesses a scimitar that dispels the brilliance of the seven suns with its rays and destroys all afflictions; she bears in her right hand a moon of shimmering nectar;

she holds in her left hand an exceedingly white lotus filled with blood, along with a banner and other emblems; her head is encircled by the goddess Kālī, who is dark as a thunderbolt; and her raised hand is released [in the gesture of granting boons]. || 2 ||
"Having the color of the twilight and vermilion," and so forth.
She is one whose color is like that of the twilight and vermilion due to the arising of great passion (*mahārāga*).

"She who has surpassed the splendor of seven suns with her mass of harsh rays": *khara* means intense; *kara* means ray. Thus, *kharakara* is an intense ray, and *kharakaranikara* is a collection or multitude of such rays. By this *kharakaranikara*, [the splendors] are *apāsta*, meaning destroyed or eclipsed.
The connection is as follows: she bears that knife which possesses the brilliance of seven suns.
She is the destroyer of all suffering—that is, the remover of every pain and affliction—and she bestows the knife of wisdom by uprooting the afflictions such as passion and the rest.

She holds with her left hand the moon, which radiates nectar and whose rays are unceasing; and with her right arm, she holds a curved knife in the right hand—this being appropriate because the sun-element resides in the right and because wisdom (*prajñā*) is sharp by nature.

Furthermore, it also demonstrates that through the joy of wisdom, the glorious *bodhicitta* has been held by me in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). This is connected to the phrase "holding a lotus."
The lotus illuminates great bliss; it is exceedingly white because its nature is the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*),
and it is filled with red because its intrinsic being is great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).

"Beginning with the banner": by means of the banner (*dhvaja*) and the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), the first [term] "great" (*mahati*) indicates the holding of the *khaṭvāṅga* within the *avadhūtī*, which is an indication of the holding of the *bodhicitta*. "By Kālī": by Kālī, who is the thunderbolt (*dambholi*). "With a head encircled by her": of what? Of the head (*mastaka*). "By her row" (*āli*): because she holds five skulls of emptiness (*śūnyapañcaka*) in that row (*āli*), the holding of *bodhicitta* in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is made manifest by this. Regarding "thunderbolt-row" (*dambholikāli*): the thunderbolt (*dambholi*) is the vajra; the thunderbolt itself is "thunderbolt-like" (*dambholika*); its row is the "thunderbolt-row" (*dambholikāli*). By that thunderbolt-row, it is "encircled," meaning known in every respect.
Her head indicates the maintenance of the mind of enlightenment endowed with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as shown by her bearing a garland of vajras on her forehead.
She has her hands raised upward; that is, she is one whose hands are released and raised upwards. (2)

Furthermore, what is she like? Her body is adorned with a garland of severed heads; blood flows from her mouth as she tastes it; she utters a loud roar; her left face is turned upward and distorted; she possesses excellent and auspicious gait; her primary face is fierce; she is full of bliss, full of passion, and endowed with various aesthetic sentiments (rasas); she dances in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka); her limbs are sealed by the six mudrās; she is divested of clothing; she is sixteen years of age; and she is a woman of exquisite form. (3)
"Her limbs adorned with a garland of severed heads," and so forth.
She is "one whose limbs are adorned with a garland of severed heads" because she maintains the *āli* (vowels) and *kāli* (consonants).
She has "blood dripping from her mouth" because blood—red in color—drips from her mouth due to her drinking the blood of emptiness from the four Māras located at her shoulders and other parts.
She whose taste is the six tastes characterized by the six flavors; she who possesses the eye of purity, meaning she has six eyes.
She has two faces, for the venerable Vajradevī has three eyes on each face, because she perceives all aspects of the three times through both the conventional and ultimate truths.
She emits a roar because she is filled with absolute bliss.

On her left side she has an upward-facing lion face, and on her right an upward-facing boar face; the assumption of the boar face is due to the purification of *saṃvṛti* (conventional reality), since *saṃvṛti* is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), and the boar is born from delusion.

She possesses excellent and auspicious gait, and her faces ending with that rooted in wrath are of a nature playful with passion (*śṛṅgāra*), as this is the primary characteristic of the principal face.

She is constantly full of bliss due to the maintenance of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); she is full of passion because of the uninterrupted arising of great passion (*mahārāga*); and she is endowed with various aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) through her connection with the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*).
She performs the dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) due to her movement within the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).

She is the one whose limbs are delighted by the six mudrās; she is called a *mudrā* because she bestows joy (*muda*) and gladness (*harṣa*). Her body is sealed with the six mudrās—the wheel, the earring, the necklace, the breast-ornament, the girdle, and the sacred thread—because of the purification of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
She is devoid of clothing because of her abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*).
She has sixteen digits because of the purity of the sixteen emptinesses;
she has beautiful limbs because the body of the Blessed Lady was produced from the accumulation of merit gathered over hundreds of thousands of eons. (3)
Having first performed the ritual procedures for summoning knowledge and so forth as before, the mantra-expert, skilled in the rules,
should meditate on a single swastika revolving rapidly toward his own forehead.
"The procedure for the summoning of gnosis," and so forth;
the connection is that one should meditate on the svastika.

Having performed the procedure for summoning the wheel of gnosis according to the stated sequence, the mantra-practitioner who knows the ritual—that is, who knows the method as it is prescribed—[should proceed].
Facing the false [object], revolving near the face of a bee like a potter's wheel—one, not two, swiftly and rapidly. || 4 ||
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the previously described rotating wheel, red and intensely blazing, within the element of space, in the excellent cave of Mount Trikūṭa.
Regarding the passage beginning with "tadanu" (thereafter):
the connection is that one should meditate on the *cakra*.

Just as previously described in the worship with vermilion (*sindūra*), the *cakra* is indicated as being completely filled with the syllables of the mantra; in exactly the same way, within the element of space—meaning within the *dharmodayā* which is endowed with the element of ether—one should meditate.
He dwells within the hollow of the Trikūṭa mountain, in the center of a three-petaled lotus, revolving like the wheel of a potter; he dwells there because of his excellence. || 5 ||
There, as if steady despite its extreme speed, like a lamp blazing in a windless place that does not flicker,
he caused the wheel of the thighs to revolve with ease, performing a libation with a flowing shower of nectar.
Regarding the passage beginning with "there, as if steady," its connection is precisely with the previously mentioned phrase "one should meditate upon that wheel.
It is "as if steady" because of the extreme velocity resulting from the intense rotation.

"It blazes like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker" is easy to understand. "It melts the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*)," meaning it causes the wheel of great bliss to liquefy; "clothed in the essence of flowing nectar," this wheel—wherein the bodhicitta is established—is situated between the anus and the genitals and should be meditated upon. Here, a brief instruction is stated: [The wheel] should be visualized as being located between the anus and the penis, clothed in the essence of the flowing nectar that results from melting the wheel of great bliss. Regarding this, a little instruction is now expressed.

First, one should diligently bring the mind endowed with passion (*sarāga-citta*) into being through the yoga of the knowledge-lotus and the vajra, by means of recollecting previously experienced bliss.

From the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*), it goes to the enjoyment wheel (*sambhoga-cakra*); from the enjoyment wheel to the dharma wheel (*dharma-cakra*); from the dharma wheel to the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇa-cakra*); from the emanation wheel to the wheel at the base of the vajra; from the wheel at the base of the vajra to the center of the vajra; and from the center of the vajra to the tip of the vajra.

When the glorious bodhicitta has reached the tip of the vajra, whatever bliss characterized by non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*) arises, one should abide in that very bliss. Then, that bodhicitta is again turned back into the *avadhūtī*.
One should cause [the disciple] to enter.
One should contemplate—that is, visualize—[the disciple] as dissolved by the vapor upon the surface of a stainless mirror.

Here, the row of colored powders (rajo-rāji) of the venerable Vajra Guru should be served; however, the *bodhicitta* must never be abandoned under any circumstances, for from its abandonment, detachment (*virāga*) would arise. Thus it is stated in the *Sekoddeśa*:
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the passion of emission,
by which the yogi attains immutable bliss from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Even a lover, due to dispassion, does not seek out the science of erotics; how much less so, then, would one do so in this Tantra? Thus it was said by me.
The yogi seeks suffering.
One should accomplish the supreme unchanging through the nature of the white (semen) changing;
[the emission] occurs in the foundation.
The fading away of passion for that which is placed upon the vessel.
The relationship between the support and the supported persists only as long as one has not attained the state of immutability;
once the mind has attained immutability, it no longer possesses the characteristics of support and supported.
And therefore, without the retention of the bodhicitta, enlightenment is not attained.

Thus it is said in the *Śrī Kālacakra*: "The entry of the vital breath into the center; the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels]; the mind reaching supreme bliss during union with the mudrā; the awakening of the vajra;
and the sound of the vajra within the lotus (or one's own [lotus])."
The sprinkling of the water of semen for the sake of bliss, the casting of the seed accompanied by pleasure, which removes the fear of death—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru.
Therefore, this alone is the means to perfect enlightenment.

Now he describes the nature of that wheel endowed with great bliss: One should perceive it as having the nature of the three bodies, supreme, consisting of the innate (*sahaja*), pervading the world, and possessing an uninterrupted stream of radiating peace; subsequently, one should perceive it facing westward. (7)
"Having the nature of the three bodies," and so forth.

Its form consists of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body. Among these, the Dharma-body transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is to be known by the Omniscient One, has emptiness as its essential nature, and is characterized by the wisdom of non-arising. The Enjoyment-body is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, and it arises from the accumulation of merit.

The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is that in which the activity of mind and mental factors has ceased, accessible only to Bodhisattvas; born from the power of skill in training those to be disciplined through the impetus of former vows, it is non-conceptual like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), fulfilling all intentions— this is its intrinsic nature,
because it is supremely and exceedingly exalted.

That which is innate (*sahaja*)—meaning that whose essential nature (*ātmasvabhāva*) is innate due to the unity of the three bodies—is called the Body of Great Bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*). That very [body] is characterized by union (*yuganaddha*), being the single flavor of the conventional and the ultimate. How is the unity of the conventional and the ultimate understood? For while the conventional has the nature of phenomena (*bhāvasvabhāva*), the ultimate has emptiness as its own form (*śūnyatāsvarūpa*).

How can there be unity between two mutually contradictory things? To this, the following response is given: The Tathāgata, while being by his own nature one whose mind and mental factors have ceased, exists as the very essence of emptiness; yet, because he appears [as having] the nature of an entity in dependence upon the minds of those to be trained, there is no contradiction, just like the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).

Well said, for it fulfills the intentions of all beings. However, [one might ask] how the body can remain when mind and mental factors have ceased? It remains because the body is dependent upon both body and mind. There is no fault here, since that which is born from the accumulation of merit remains throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and likewise, by the power of the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), there may again be the cessation of mind and mental factors.

Therefore, one should see—that is, perceive—all things as being established in their own nature (*svastha*). For this very reason, they are all-pervasive throughout the entire world. Indeed, because every entity possesses the nature of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*), it consists of a continuous flow of manifesting and infinite peace; and because its nature is non-perishing, it is the meaning of "eternal bliss" while manifesting. One should perceive it, which means one should discern it. Facing backward—that is, directed toward the immediate present—is because it is possible to discern it right there.
Next, he explains the application to the cultivation of bliss. || 7 ||
One should meditate upon this every day, at each junction of the day, or whenever there is leisure; this is clearly stated [to be practiced] until the signs of accomplishment appear. 8.
"Every day," and so forth;
the connection is with the word "one should contemplate.
This aforementioned great bliss (*mahāsukha*) [should be contemplated] every day or at each junction of the day (*pratisandhya*).

Whenever the wind enters the *avadhūtī*—meaning at the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), or at every moment, or indeed always—until the sign of accomplishment arises; "accomplishment" refers to *mahāmudrā*, and "sign" means its cause. Until that occurs, one should clearly meditate upon it everywhere.
First, this sign of accomplishment, which will be described below, is stated. (8)

Thus it is said: "When this [state] becomes manifest and is clearly cultivated through the continuous flow of joy and absorption that arises effortlessly, then there will be no sensation even when struck by a whip or a slap; at that time, perfection is not far off. (9)
"Born of effortlessness" means that through uninterrupted practice, joy arises without effort because it is no longer followed by exertion; due to its stability,
this [joy] becomes clearly manifested and becomes more distinct.

Regarding this, it is said: "When struck by a whip, a slap, and so forth, there is no sensation. If, when one strikes oneself with a whip, a leather strap, a slap, a blow of the hand, or the like, no painful sensation occurs, then it should be understood that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is not far off;
that is, accomplishment has become imminent. || 9 ||

He states another sign: "If the sharp sound of beaten drums and other instruments is not within the range of hearing, then for one who possesses meditative concentration, unsurpassed and supreme enlightenment is attained, and the highest accomplishment is swiftly realized even in a dream. (10)
Regarding the passage beginning with "pratāḍitānām":

when instruments such as the *paṇava*—the term "*paṇava-mardala-ādi*" including the *dakkā*, *bherī*, and so forth—are struck intensely (*prakarṣeṇa*) and in a great manner (*mahatā prakāreṇa*), their sharp resonance (*paṭudhvani*) or loud sound does not come within the range of hearing; that is, it does not become an object of auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).

He states another sign: when the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment is attained—even in every dream—if the yogi sees himself as a perfectly awakened Buddha (samyaksambuddha), then for that practitioner of meditation, the supreme accomplishment will soon be realized. Thus, for the yogi engaged in the cultivation of great bliss, the supreme accomplishment, which is the state of Vajradhara, will certainly occur. || 10 ||

Having observed the signs of accomplishment, he states what must then be done: "Having seen the signs of accomplishment in a cemetery, a mountain thicket, at the foot of a tree, or similar places, the wise one, dwelling there, should constantly practice the yoga born of the utpannakrama. (11)
"Having seen," and so forth.

The wise one should practice the yoga of the generation stage; the meaning is that he should meditate upon great bliss. "Unceasingly" means continuously, in a cemetery, a mountain grove, at the foot of a tree, and so on—where "cemetery" (*pitṛvana*) refers to a charnel ground, "mountain" (*giri*) to a peak, and "grove" (*kuñja*) to a bower of creepers.
The root of a tree is easily accessible.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes empty houses and so forth. Dwelling and staying in such a place, the yogi shall immediately realize the meditative absorption of great bliss (*mahāsukha-samādhi*) due to the absence of mental distraction.
Regarding what occurs when meditative absorption is accomplished, he says: "When the earth and the other elements are mastered, they dissolve in successive order."
Then there appears that which resembles the sky, luminous, consisting of mere gnosis, and real. (12)
Regarding the passage beginning with "siddhau" and so forth:

the dissolution (*laya*) of the earth and the other elements occurs in a successive order; that is, the dissolution of earth, water, fire, air, consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the rest is accomplished.
Among these, the earth element dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into the mind (*citta*), and the mind into the intellect (*cetana*).
When mental ignorance [subsides] within ignorance, that ignorance also dissolves into the luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*).
Thus it has been said: "The earth element dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire;
fire dissolves into the subtle element; and wind dissolves into the mind."
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, and the mental factors into ignorance;
that too goes into the luminous—this is cessation within the three realms of existence.

If this were so, what would be the case? At that time, cessation—which is like the sky, resembling space because all conceptual constructions have departed—is luminous, stainless, mere gnosis (*jñānamātra*), and like an illusion; for this very reason, it is said to be truly supreme. Here it is asked: "When everything has ceased, how can even gnosis remain, since it is dependent upon an object of knowledge (*jñeya*)?

It should not be said [that gnosis does not remain], for what is intended here is mere gnosis characterized by emptiness—empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnya*), like an illusion, and devoid of the mind of conceptual construction (*vikalpamanas*). That [gnosis] is not negated in this context.

And so it was said by the glorious Lord Śākya: "Just as the blackness of copper is destroyed through the application of mercury, yet its essential nature (sattva) is not destroyed because it remains in a state of purity;
in the same way, the impurities of the mind are destroyed through the yoga of emptiness."
The nature of that gnosis, which exists in a state of purity, is not destroyed;
therefore, there indeed exists mere gnosis whose intrinsic nature is emptiness.
Upon the arising of that gnosis, first, signs corresponding to the object appear. (12)
One should recognize it by its signs; those who know it understand that the signs are fivefold.
Therefore, the yogi, being composed, should perceive them with the mind.
"One should know," and so forth.
Knowledge without mind is [known] by means of signs (*cihna*) and marks (*nimitta*).

As for how many those signs are, "those who know" (*tajjñaḥ*)—meaning those who understand them—are aware that the signs are of five kinds. For that very reason, the yogin endowed with meditative absorption (*samādhi*) should perceive those signs with the mind.
The signs arise in succession. || 13 ||
Regarding that, he states the sequence: "First, the sign appears like a mirage; the second has the form of smoke;
the third is like fireflies; the fourth is clearly radiant like a lamp. (14)

"First," and so forth. The first sign is like a mirage; the second sign has the form of smoke; the third is clearly like fireflies; and the fourth is like a lamp, shining like the flame of a light, distinct and manifest. || 14 ||
He states the fifth sign: "The fifth sign is luminous and non-conceptual, resembling a cloudless sky.
Having thus attained the sign, one obtains the Great Mudrā. (15)
"Free from" means like a sky free from clouds, like a stainless space;
it is luminous (*prabhāsvara*).
At that moment, it is non-conceptual due to the cessation of mind and mental factors.

Thus, having obtained the sign (*nimitta*) and attained the sign through the stated sequence, the yogin attains the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). The meaning is that he shall directly realize emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects. || 15 ||

Desiring to rise, the knower of yoga, possessing the intellect of reality, should prostrate to the Yoginī and the Lord, utter "mūḥ" while remaining still, and having risen, perform his duties; he should always remain joined with the pair of yogas.
"Desiring to arise," and so forth.

When one wishes to arise from that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then, having prostrated to and paid homage to the Yoginī Vajravārāhī, and having invoked the Lord situated upon the head by uttering the syllable *mūḥ*—that is, reciting the mantra *mūḥ*—one who possesses the wisdom of reality (*tattvadhīḥ*) should rise and perform his duties. One should always abide with the intellect free from intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), through the union of yoga (*yogayuga*) characterized by the ego-identity of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*), which is the gnosis of the great bliss of meditative absorption (*yogavinmahāsukhasamādhijñāna*).

Thus ends the second chapter, the Procedure for Meditation, in the *Mahāsukhaprakāśikā* (The Illumination of Great Bliss), composed by the monk Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Middle Way, for the sake of perfecting the knowledge of reality.
[The Procedure for Favoring Disciples] Having been entreated many times by disciples who have formed a maṇḍala and bowed at his lotus feet,
the mantra-master should bestow favor upon them on the tenth lunar day.
Now, for the purpose of initiating disciples, it is said:
"Being requested," and so forth.

"Requested" means entreated many times, in various ways, by disciples who have formed a maṇḍala—that is, those by whom a maṇḍala has been constructed; the Guru is to be requested preceded by the construction of a maṇḍala.

One should bestow grace—that is, show compassion—toward those disciples who have bowed at her lotus feet, whose speech is free from idle chatter, and who abide by the mantra born of the Blessed Lady on the tenth lunar day, and not on any other date. || 1 ||
Having worshipped the Goddess in the form of the mantra residing within the wheel, and having performed the yoga,
one who has recited the mantra should take up the supreme primordial [substance] and emerge from that place.
"Having worshipped her in the form of the mantra," and so forth.
Having worshipped the Goddess, who is the very nature of the mantra as described in the section on the worship with vermilion (sindūra), he says this very thing:

"situated in the wheel" means situated in the six-spoked wheel; "one who has performed yoga" means one who has achieved meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), or else one whose form is non-different from the Blessed Lady.

Having taken and grasped [the substance] consecrated with mantra, one should purify it with the Bhagavatī mantra. One should then depart from that place of worship of the Bhagavatī. This is what is meant: the Bhagavatī is worshipped, and the cloth-painting (paṭa) and so forth belonging to the end of the tantra must be offered; then, having worshipped the Bhagavatī, one should take the substance purified by mantra from that location and go outside.
The intention is that it is for the sake of the disciples. || 2 ||

Then the Guru should look upon the disciple— who has performed the five circumambulations, stands with palms joined, has offered the prescribed fee, and holds a garland of flowers— as the Lord Dhyātakanātha.
"Then," and so forth;
the connection is that he should look at the disciple.
This means [he should look at] one who has performed prostration with the two knees, the two hands, and the head, having arranged the five maṇḍalas as prescribed.

Standing above him is he to whom the sacrificial fee was given, who has renounced all his possessions, and who wears a garland of flowers—holding a flower wreath with both hands; upon whose head the Lord, the Guru—the meaning being the Vajra-Guru—is meditated. || 3 ||
Thereafter, having meditated upon the aforementioned circle of goddesses as radiating rays with great speed,
the wielder of the vajra should bestow it upon the body of the resident disciple.
Regarding the passage beginning with *tadanu* and so forth:

immediately thereafter, having meditated upon—that is, having visualized—the aforementioned wheel of the Goddess (*devīcakra*), which has six spokes, is filled with the syllables of the mantra, emits rising rays, flashes with radiance, and revolves with great speed—one should then bestow it upon the body of the resident disciple. "The resident" refers to the disciple; his "body" refers to the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*). What should be done after that? One should give it to the Vajra-holder; at that time, one should give the full vessel to the disciple.
And the disciple must consume it all;
that is the instruction regarding the "intoxicant" (madana). || 4 ||
Thus there may be possession, agitation, trembling, tears, falling [down],
the arising of knowledge, and also the attainment of one's own true nature, according to the sequence. (5)
"Thus," and so forth.
By this sequence, the descent (*āveśa*) occurs; therein, the descent is threefold: the descent of body, the descent of speech, and the descent of mind.

Among these, in the descent of body, there is a surge of emotion, horripilation, trembling of the limbs, and the shedding of tears of joy, as one falls to the ground. In the descent of mind, there is the arising of gnosis (*jñāna*) and the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-pratibhāna*).
In the case of the descent of speech (*vāgāveśa*), there would be an unprecedented proclamation; it is similar and concordant with the demonstration of the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
He speaks in a manner that is similar, following a sequence and in due order.
Or else, if even in this way the descent does not occur for one of meager merit, then this ritual procedure must be performed.

One should consecrate the five limbs of a goat with the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas; one should prepare equal portions together with great oil and great guggulu incense. With that, incense should be offered using the mantra of Vārāhī. It is certain that by merely smelling it, possession occurs. || 5 ||

Thereafter, one should explain the samādhi and the worship mantra of Vajrayoginī to one who is endowed with faith, virtuous, and possesses true devotion toward the Guru as non-different from the Buddha. (6)
Regarding the passage beginning with *tadanu* and so forth:
"he should explain the samādhi" means the samādhi of great bliss (*mahāsukha*);
and [he should explain] the worship mantra of Vajrayoginī.

To one who is endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, and wise—one who has true devotion toward the Guru as inseparable from the Buddha, because of the non-duality of those two—such a person may be told this yoga, which provides immediate conviction and is well-proven.
However, it should not be told to a disciple whose mind is devoid of faith and who lacks devotion. (7)
"He shall not speak," and so forth.

He shall not speak—that is, he shall not reveal—this yoga, the aforementioned samādhi which produces immediate conviction (*sadyaḥ-pratyaya*), which generates trust through a friend (*mitra*), and which bestows excellent accomplishment (*susiddhi*); for "excellent accomplishment" refers to Mahāmudrā, and [the yoga] gives that. [This applies] to a disciple whose mind is devoid of faith, whose heart has abandoned faith, and who is bereft of devotion. (7)
Now, having seen [the benefits], he speaks again of the advantages: "But for him who performs worship of the circle of goddesses conjoined with mantra, his eight fears and great sins depart. (8)
"He performs," and so forth.

For whoever performs the mantra-worship of the goddess-cakra—the six-spoked cakra of the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, joined with mantras and complete with mantras—for him the eight fears depart; the fears of lions, elephants, fire, snakes, thieves, fetters, and water depart, and even great sins, including the five actions of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), flee away. (8)
Misfortune, poverty, disease, old age, suffering, and dejection;
delusion, strife, impurity, and afflictions, as well as various kinds of torments. (9)

"Unfortunate," and so forth. In this world, one becomes endowed with supreme good fortune; [the following] depart: poverty (dāridrya), which is lack of wealth; disease (vyādhi), which is bodily affliction; old age (jarā), which is decrepitude; suffering (duḥkha), which is physical sensation (kāyikī vedanā); dejection (daurmanasya), which is mental sensation (caitasikī vedanā);

delusion (bhrama), which is error; strife (kali), which is dispute; turbidity (kaluṣa), which is sin; the afflictions (kleśa), namely passion, hatred, and delusion; and the disturbances caused by planetary spirits (graha) and the like—of various kinds (nānāvidha) and many sorts (anekaprakāra)—this is the connection with the word "depart. || 9 ||
He who recites the Cakra-mantra while meditating upon it in his heart with speech restrained attains the eight siddhis, as well as the five superknowledges and the eight qualities.
"He who recites," and so forth.

Having meditated upon—that is, having visualized—the *cakramantra*, the mantra together with the *cakra*, within his heart by means of the "speech of restraint" (*nirodhavāc*) through the mind, that practitioner of mantra attains the eight accomplishments (*siddhi*): the accomplishment of collyrium, pills, sandals, medicinal herbs, jewels, mantras, yakṣa-women, and entry into the bodies of others;

the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), namely divine hearing, divine sight, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of former abodes, and the cognition of miraculous powers (*ṛddhivijñāna*); and likewise the eight qualities (*guṇa*): minuteness (*aṇimā*), lightness (*laghimā*), heaviness (*garimā*), lordship (*īśitva*), and mastery (*vaśitva*).
Agency, the state of being an object of enjoyment, and the arising of desire and its fulfillment—these are the eight qualities. || 10 ||
He who meditates with effort every day at the four junctions of the day upon her whose face is like a crow, conquers death—which cannot be overcome even by Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā. (11)
"Contemplating," and so forth:

that mantra-practitioner who daily contemplates with effort Kiravaktrā, the boar-faced one (Kolāsyā), during the four junctions of the day—namely at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight—he conquers death, that passing away which is impossible for Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha to overcome. || 11 ||

For him who meditates upon the goddess Aśanikolamukhī together with her wheel, there arise vast lands with clothing, food, drink, wealth, and grain, as well as palaces, divine beds, seats, and all necessary implements; moreover, various beloved sciences are produced for him.
Thus concludes the procedure for favoring the disciple, together with its benefits, for the sake of perfecting the knowledge of reality.

"Garments, food," and so forth. Garments mean clothing; food means rice and the like; drink means milk and the like; wealth means gold and the like; grain means rice and the like; vast land means a great expanse of earth; a palace means a divine residence; a divine bed means a mattress and the like;
a seat means a lion-throne and the like; and implements mean couches and the like—all these belong to that practitioner of mantra.

Beloved celestial women, various sciences, and diverse arts and crafts—all these belong to him who meditates upon her whose face is like a thunderbolt-mallet, who has a vajra-mallet for a mouth, who possesses a wheel, and who is endowed with two wheels, one above and one below.
Thus ends the "Method for Assisting Disciples along with its Benefits" from the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhiṭīkā* composed by the monk Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Madhyamaka.

[The Method for Extracting the Mantra] Now, therefore, the secret of the mantra—the extraction of the mantra transmitted through the lineage of gurus—is written: Hereafter, I shall declare the extraction of the mantra, which is the heart of Vajrayoginī.
Thus, it has been transmitted from ear to ear and from mouth to mouth in succession.
"Mantra," and so forth.

Hereafter, immediately following what was previously stated, I shall describe—that is, I will speak of—the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), which is the heart-essence of Vajrayoginī and the heart-essence of Kolamukhī, which has come from ear to ear, having been transmitted through a succession of ears, because it must be kept strictly secret. (1)
Having drawn a wheel as previously described, provided with the abode of the hosts of Maruts,
one should there, following the sequence, write the vowels and consonants (ālikāli) in the same manner in the corners.
"Beginning with 'pūrva' and so forth":
having drawn the wheel in the form of the *dharmodaya* as if it were previously mentioned or previously described;

one should write the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) there in that wheel, according to the sequence and in proper order, provided with the abode of the hosts of Maruts, consisting of forty-nine squares.
Starting from the vowel *a* up to the sixteenth vowel (*au*), and starting from the consonant *ka* up to *ha*;
for this very reason, the sequence of the triangular expansion (*trikoṇaprastāra*) is described:
"One, three, likewise five, seven, and especially nine."
The tenth characteristic of the internal cavities is joined with three times eleven.
The wise one should write [the letters] there in sequence, one above the other; having made them empty by means of the letter *kṣa*, he should place the *āli* and *kāli*.

The extraction of the syllables is now being described: Having first written the triad consisting of the letter below *zha*, the one situated below *ḍa*, and that adorned by the one below *ha*—joined together—the six-syllable mantra illuminates the principles (*tattva*).
Regarding *zhādharaga* and so forth:
"that which is below the letter *zha*" (*zhādharaga*) refers to the letter *a*; one should write that *a*. This connection applies everywhere.

"That which stands below the letter *ḍa*" (*ḍādharastha*) refers to the letter *u*; it is "adorned by that which is below the letter *ha*" (*hādharagavibhūṣita*), meaning it is joined with and adorned by the letter *m*, which is "below the letter *ha*" (*hādharaga*). [Thus, the letters *a* and *u* are joined with *m*.]
When there is a conjunction, the vowel *o* is adorned with the letter *m*; thus, the meaning is the syllable *oṃ*. Having first written this triad, [it is said]:
*oṃ oṃ oṃ*, which illuminates the reality of the six syllables and reveals the supreme reality of the syllables. (3)
The letter *bha* joined with the one situated above [the letter *cha*],
and then the letter *ṭa* situated above [the letter *cha*] should be written;
[then] the letter *ḍa* joined with the one below [the letter *ṣa*], the letter *ṣa* situated below [the letter *śa*], and the letter *śa* joined with the one situated above [the letter *ṣa*].

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhordhvaga" and so forth: the letter *sa*, which is situated above the letter *bha*, is joined with the letter *ba*, which is situated above the letter *cha*; thereafter, the letter *ra*, which is situated above the letter *ṭa*, should be written. (va)

Joined with the lower part of *ḍa* (*u*), [one takes] the letter *ba*, which is situated below *ṣa* (*bu*). Joined with that which is situated above *ṣa* (*dha*), [one takes] the letter *da*, which is positioned above *śa* (*ddha*). || 4 ||
First is the letter situated below *ṇa* and above *la*; next is that which is positioned above and joined with the letter below *ṭa*;
then that which is joined with the letter above *ṭha* and accompanied by the one below it; and finally, that which is joined with *ai* and situated within *ha* and *ṭa*.

"Ñādharādi" and so forth: joined with the lower part of *ña* (*ñādharayutam*), which is the vowel *ā* situated below *ña*; joined with that, the letter *ḍa* (written as *ḍā*) situated at the base of *lṛ*;

joined with the lower part of *ṭa* (*ṭādharayutam*), the letter *ka* situated above *pa*; and following that, joined with the vowel *i*, which is the lower part of *ṭa*, the letter *ka* situated above *pa* (forming *ki*).

[The mantra is formed as follows: The letter *ṇa* (ṭha) joined with the downward-moving vowel *ī* (the lower part of *ṭha*), together with the upward-moving letter *na* (the upper part of *pha*)—thus (*nī*).
Then the left side of *ai* (the vowel *e*), situated thereon, followed by the letter *ya*, which stands between the letters *ha* and *ṭa* (*ye*). || 5 ||
The letter *ca* situated in the middle of the house (*ha*), joined with the right-hand *tha*, well-established below *bha*;
thereafter, the letter *ha* situated in the middle of the hand (*sa*), joined with the left-hand *ta*, and subsequently the letter *ṭha* situated in the middle of the house (*ha*). || 6 ||

One should write the letter *ba* situated between *ca* and *ka*; it is joined with the *ṭha* on its right and well-positioned below the *bha*. Following that, there is the letter *ra* located to the right of the *ṭha*, joined with which [the *ba*] is well-positioned below the *bha*. Then there is the letter *ja*, well-positioned below the *bha*.
(jra)
The letter *va*, situated between the letters *ha* and *tha*;

joined with the letter to the left of *ta* (i.e., *na*), which is itself situated between *ṭha* and *la* and joined with the letter to the left of *ta* (i.e., *ṇa*); and the letter *ra*, situated between the letters *ṭha* and *la*. (ṇṇa) || 6 ||
The end of all the consonants (kṣa),

the middle of the third group (ṭha) joined with the vowel from the left (ī), the letter following ṇa (ṇa) joined with the vowel above (ū), the letter below la (la) joined with the vowel above (ū), and the letter below tha (tha) joined with the vowel on the right (e). (7)
The end of all digits (*sarvakalānta*) is *aḥ*; the letter *fa* and the letter *na* are between them; the first of the third group (*tṛtīyavargādi*) is *ṭa*, and its leftward [vowel] is *i*.
Together with that, it is *nī*.
The letter *la* below, joined with the upper [vowel]— that is, the letter *ya* situated below *la*, accompanied by the letter *e* above the letter *ṇa*;
and the letter *va* situated above the letter *cha*.

The letter *ja*, which is the base of the letter *bha* and joined with the right side of the letter *ṭha*; and the letter *ra*, which is the right side of the letter *ṭha* and joined with that [same base]—(jra). || 7 ||
The letter *ṭa* below joined with *ūrdhvaga* (*ra*), the letter *tha* below joined with *ūrdhvaga* (*ra*), and then the letter *ṇa* below;
the letter *fa* below joined with the letter *ṭha* below (*ba*), situated above *for* (*ma*), and the letter *la* below joined with *ṇa* above (*ṇa*). || 8 ||
The letter *ba* below the letter *ṣa*, joined with the letter *ai* above the letter *ta*; then the letter *tha* above, joined with the letter *ṇa* below;
then the letter *ra* below the letter *ṇa*, joined with the letter *au* above the letter *tha*;
and finally the letter *ca* below the letter *fa*.

Joined with the lower part of *ṭha* [the letter *ṛ*], joined with the *ī* situated below the letter *ṭha*, joined with the *na* situated above the letter *fa*, joined with the upper part of *ṇa* and the lower part of *la* [the letter *e*], and joined with the *ya* situated below the letter *la*: (*ye*). || 8 ||
Accompanied by the lower *ḍa* and the void (*śūnya*), with three folds and the jewel-seat (*ratnalam*) situated above;
joined with the lower *tha*, located on the lower *śa*, and also conjoined with the lower *ña*. || 9 ||
The syllable *huṃ* consists of the letter *ha*, which is joined with the letter below *ḍa* (*u*) and the void (*anusvāra*).
That triad (*huṃ huṃ huṃ*) is positioned above the letter *ca*, specifically above the letter *fa*.
*Ratalaṃ* and *refatalaṃ* should be understood as the three *faṭ*s (*faṭ faṭ faṭ*) through the combination of the letter *ṭ*.

It is joined with the lower part of *th*, the lower part of *ś*, and the lower part of *ñ*; furthermore, it is accompanied by the letter *va*, which is the lower part of *th*, together with the letter *sa*, which is the lower part of *ś*, and also joined with the lower part of *ñ*;
that is to say, it is joined with the vowel *ā*, which is the lower part of *ñ*—meaning [the syllable] *svā*. || 9 ||
This secret mantra of the goddess Aśanidevī, composed of the syllables *sa*, *ya*, *ma*, *dha*, *ga*, *ṃ*, *zha*, *vā*, *ma*, *ga*, *sa*, and *me*, should be written, recited, and meditated upon. 10.

The meaning is: the letter *ha* situated between *sa* and *ka*, accompanied by the letter *zha*—that is, the letter *ha* located between the letters *sa* and *ka*, together with the letter *a* on the left side of the letter *zha* (*hā*).

This secret [mantra] is formed from the aforementioned syllables; having been drawn forth from the first syllable *ka* which was formed by those stated syllables, because it is the cause of that secret, what is this secret? It is this mantra of Aśanidevī—that is to say, the mantra of Vajravārāhī. As for what should be done with this mantra, he says: "It is to be written, recited, and meditated upon."
It should be written, recited, and meditated upon. || 10 ||
The wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial tree, the peak of Mount Meru, the water-pot of plenty, and even the illustrious cow of plenty are all highly praised;
yet while those, when being cultivated, bestow wealth here, this [practice] bestows happiness along with wealth.
Thus ends the procedure for the extraction of mantras in the accomplishment of the knowledge of reality.
"Intention-jewel," and so forth: the *cintāmaṇi* jewel,

the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the foremost vase (*agraghaṭa*), the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), and the glorious wish-granting cow (*śrīkāmadhenu*)— whatever other things are praised and renowned, when they are accomplished, they bestow wealth.

In this world, moreover, this king of mantras bestows supramundane bliss, that is, great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "With wealth" means accompanied by riches; other [mantras], when accomplished, give only wealth and not unsurpassed bliss, but this one grants everything. Therefore, in every respect, this alone—
For the sake of accomplishing all desired aims at all times, and as the cause for mundane and supramundane accomplishments, it should be cultivated by Bodhisattvas in the world. || 11 ||

Thus ends the procedure for the extraction of mantras in the *Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi-ṭīkā* composed by the monk Śrī Dhyānacandra, who delights in the Madhyamaka. [The Self-Consecration] In this [work], which was written according to the ritual rules upon a leaf for the purpose of worship by one who knows the rites, the protection of a child should be performed according to the rule by binding [the mantra] on the arms, the neck, the topknot, and the forearm. (1)
Regarding the verse beginning with *yasmin*:

In which [mirror] this King of Mantras has been inscribed according to the ritual for the purpose of worship by practitioners who know the procedure; in that [mirror], the protection of the child must be performed according to rule—the protection of the infant should be carried out preceded by the worship of the Goddess. With that [mirror] bound [to the body] along with the mantra, [the child should be protected] with vermilion (*sindūra*) on the arm, the neck, and the crest—on the arm, the neck, and the topknot. || 1 ||
Upon seeing him, serpents flee along with spirits, seizing demons, and hosts of piśācas;
and other terrifying beings who cause fear and distress to children, like forest-dwellers fleeing in terror from a powerful lion. (2)
"Having seen," and so forth: *bhujagāḥ* means serpents; they flee, that is, they run away.

Having seen the child together with the protective charm (*sarakṣam*), even the *bhūtas*, *grahas*, and night-stalkers (*niśicarāḥ*), as well as the hosts of *piśācas*, flee; and others too—such as *ḍākinīs* and the like—who cause fear and distress to children, who are most terrifying and exceedingly fearsome.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: just as forest-dwelling deer and other animals, seeing a lion, flee in fear and run away;
what kind of lion? One who is "balinam," meaning powerful; and what kind of forest-dwellers flee? Being "bhayārtāḥ," that is, afflicted by fear. || 2 ||
Having received the authentic instruction and having gained conviction in yoga, this perfection— abiding in the radiance of stainless knowledge— has been fully described.

"Having attained" (saṃprāpya): the connection is that "this perfection has been fully described. Having attained—that is, having properly received the authentic instruction—and having seen the conviction regarding this yoga, namely, having observed the realization of this blessed yoga, [one attains] abiding in flashing, stainless knowledge.
Because its nature is radiant light, knowledge is stainless; since all afflictions have ceased, its abode is the state of *saṃvitti*.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining that [state], one should serve the lotus feet of the true guru with conciliation,
through the practice of giving, by means of physical austerities, and with prostrations.
"Therefore," and so forth.

For this very reason, in order to attain that [state] and to obtain its instruction, one must properly serve—that is, correctly propitiate—the lotus-feet of the true guru who has attained the *nimitta*. This means the complete propitiation of the guru through conciliation (*sāman*), that is, with a friendly disposition; or else, by the method of giving, such as the offering of excellent garments; or by bodily austerities, or by prostrations—in short, by every possible means. || 4 ||

May the worlds—purified of the stains of the Kali age and possessing pure enlightenment—become recipients of that supreme accomplishment of the knowledge of reality, which, like a mother in this world, gives birth to manifold benefit for sentient beings; and by means of the merit and demerit I have accumulated, bright as the rays of the full moon, may they obtain the noble *mudrā* that pacifies the fear of cyclic existence and accomplishes the welfare of all beings.
This concludes the *Svādhiṣṭhāna* [chapter], titled "The Accomplishment of the Knowledge of Reality" (*Tattvajñānasiddhi*).
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of reality," and so forth:
